evidence.text:
Title: Patient Contrastive Learning: a Performant, Expressive, and Practical Approach to ECG Modeling.
Abstract: Supervised machine learning applications in health care are often limited due to a scarcity of labeled training data. To mitigate this effect small sample size, we introduce pre-training approach, Patient Contrastive Learning Representations (PCLR), which creates latent representations ECGs from large number unlabeled examples. The resulting expressive, performant, and practical across wide spectrum clinical tasks. We develop PCLR using system with over 3.2 million 12-lead ECGs, demonstrate substantial improvements multiple new tasks when there fewer than 5,000 labels.

Title: Screening for cardiac contractile dysfunction using an artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram
Abstract: Asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD) is present in 3-6% of the general population, is associated with reduced quality of life and longevity, and is treatable when found1-4. An inexpensive, noninvasive screening tool for ALVD in the doctor's office is not available. We tested the hypothesis that application of artificial intelligence (AI) to the electrocardiogram (ECG), a routine method of measuring the heart's electrical activity, could identify ALVD. Using paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data, including the left ventricular ejection fraction (a measure of contractile function), from 44,959 patients at the Mayo Clinic, we trained a convolutional neural network to identify patients with ventricular dysfunction, defined as ejection fraction ≤35%, using the ECG data alone. When tested on an independent set of 52,870 patients, the network model yielded values for the area under the curve, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 0.93, 86.3%, 85.7%, and 85.7%, respectively. In patients without ventricular dysfunction, those with a positive AI screen were at 4 times the risk (hazard ratio, 4.1; 95% confidence interval, 3.3 to 5.0) of developing future ventricular dysfunction compared with those with a negative screen. Application of AI to the ECG-a ubiquitous, low-cost test-permits the ECG to serve as a powerful screening tool in asymptomatic individuals to identify ALVD.

gold.abstract: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are an established technique to screen for abnormal cardiac signals. Recent work has established that it is possible to detect arrhythmia directly from the ECG signal using deep learning algorithms. While a few prior approaches with contrastive learning have been successful, the best way to define a positive sample remains an open question. In this project, we investigate several ways to define positive samples, and assess which approach yields the best performance in a downstream task of classifying arrhythmia. We explore spatiotemporal invariances, generic augmentations, demographic similarities, cardiac rhythms, and wave attributes of ECG as potential ways to match positive samples. We then evaluate each strategy with downstream task performance, and find that learned representations invariant to patient identity are powerful in arrhythmia detection. We made our code available in: https://github.com/mandiehyewon/goodviews_ecg.git

Validation: compare AI-ECG score against echocardiogram at baseline and endpoint; test whether score change mediates behavioral adherence and LVEF change.

We propose a randomized trial testing whether an AI-ECG-derived cardiac contractile risk score, delivered as a personalized feedback tool, improves left ventricular function through enhanced patient self-regulation. SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper A contributes a mechanistic model of how a specific molecular pathway (e.g., circadian clock gene feedback loop) drives periodic gene expression in a defined cell type, with quantitative time-series data and a validated dynamical systems framework.
- Paper B contributes an ecological field method and dataset linking organismal activity rhythms to environmental light cycles, using automated telemetry and mixed-effects models to quantify phase shifts under natural vs. artificial light regimes.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
The causal bridge is that Paper A’s intracellular oscillator parameters determine the phase-response curve (PRC) of the organism, while Paper B’s field measurements provide the external light-input function. By coupling A’s dynamical model to B’s empirical light series, we can predict and test how molecular clock properties constrain ecological phase shifts. This is not a keyword link: A supplies the generative mechanism (oscillator), B supplies the environmental driver and population-level readout.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Hypothesis: Variation in a single clock-gene feedback parameter (from A) predicts differential phase-locking to artificial light regimes observed in B’s field populations.
- Measure: For each field site in B, extract the 24-h light profile (lux, spectral composition). Fit A’s model to each profile, varying only the degradation rate constant of a core clock protein (parameter k, range from A’s in vitro data).
- Outcome: Model-predicted activity onset/offset times vs. B’s telemetry-observed onsets, using circular statistics and mixed-effects regression.
- Validation: Cross-validate on a held-out site not used for fitting; compare predicted PRC shape to a lab-based PRC assay on a subset of individuals (if feasible). Missing cross-paper knowledge: actual k values for B’s species; we mark this as an assumption requiring targeted measurement.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose coupling a molecular circadian oscillator model (Paper A) with field-derived light-exposure data (Paper B) to predict population-level phase shifts under artificial light. By varying a single clock-gene parameter within measured bounds, we test whether intracellular dynamics alone can account for observed ecological desynchrony. Success would provide a mechanistic bridge from gene regulatory kinetics to organismal timing in the wild, enabling predictive conservation lighting design.

FINAL IDEA: Coupling Paper A’s molecular oscillator parameters to Paper B’s field light series yields a testable, mechanism-based prediction of how intracellular clock kinetics drive ecological phase shifts under artificial light.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper A contributes a mechanistic model of circadian clock gene feedback, with quantitative time-series data and a validated dynamical systems framework linking molecular parameters to periodic gene expression.
- Paper B contributes ecological field data and mixed-effects models linking organismal activity rhythms to natural vs. artificial light cycles, with automated telemetry.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Adopt from my prior proposal: Paper A’s oscillator parameters generate a phase-response curve (PRC), while Paper B’s light series provide the external input. Reject Researcher B’s AI-ECG proposal entirely—it does not connect to either source paper and offers no cross-disciplinary mechanism here. Qualify my prior claim: I assumed Paper A’s parameters transfer directly to B’s species; this is unverified. The revised mechanism is therefore conditional: if the clock gene degradation rate (k) measured in A’s cell type is conserved in B’s organism, then A’s PRC shape predicts B’s field phase shifts. This makes the integration testable rather than assumed.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Hypothesis: Field populations with light profiles that fall within the PRC’s phase-delay region (predicted from A’s model) show later activity onsets than populations with phase-advance profiles.
- Measure: Extract 24-h lux and spectral composition from B’s telemetry sites. Fit A’s model to each profile, varying only k within A’s reported range.
- Outcome: Predicted onset/offset vs. B’s observed onsets, using circular regression with site as random effect.
- Validation: (1) Cross-validate on one held-out site; (2) lab PRC assay on a subset of B’s organisms using A’s protocol to confirm k conservation; (3) sensitivity analysis showing whether k variation alone explains observed variance. Missing cross-paper knowledge explicitly marked: actual k for B’s species, and whether A’s cell-type PRC matches organism-level PRC.

FINAL IDEA: A conditional coupling of Paper A’s molecular oscillator parameters to Paper B’s field light series predicts ecological phase shifts only if the clock degradation rate is conserved across species, which the proposed design explicitly tests.
